items.summary: The Supreme Court recently upheld the reopening of income-tax assessments against businessmen Chetan Sabharwal and Nitin Sabharwal, sons of former Chief Justice of India late YK Sabharwal , over share transactions involving a total consideration of ₹255 crore [ Chetan Sabharwal v. ACIT, New Delhi ]. A Bench of Justices JB Pardiwala and K Vinod Chandran dismissed four appeals filed by the brothers challenging a 2019 Delhi High Court judgment that had upheld the Income Tax (IT) Department’s decision to reopen their assessments. The Court held that an investigation report pointing to the alleged overvaluation of shares constituted tangible material on the basis of which the Assessing Officer could form a reason to believe that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment. "The expression 'reason to believe' in Section 147 of the Act means cause or justification. The Assessing Officer must have tangible material having a rational connection or a live link with the formation of the belief... At the stage of the notice, the only question is whether there was relevant material on which a reasonable person could have formed the requisite belief, and the sufficiency of the reasons is not a justiciable issue," the Court ruled. items.title: Delhi Police seeks to silence digital rights groups IFF, SFLC on X, wants accounts removed
items.summary: The Delhi police has issued two notices to social media platform X, seeking the removal of the accounts of digital rights organisations Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) and Software Freedom Law Center (SFLC) apart from the operator of GeoBlockedIndia, over allegations of defamation against the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS). IFF is a digital rights advocacy organisation that defends against threats to civil liberties and democracy in India, and SFLC is a donor-supported legal services and policy organisation founded in 2010 that protects digital freedom, privacy and civil liberties in India. The IFF on Tuesday, November 3, said it would approach the court if the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, which also seek removal of 37 posts, including content published by 16 other users. IFF said it received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of November 3. The notices were filed by the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, on October 31 and November 2, 2026. According to IFF, the first notice was submitted to X on October 31 at 8.06 pm. It identified two posts published by IFF and SFLC on October 30 concerning a legal notice purportedly issued on behalf of the RSS. The Delhi Police reportedly described the posts as “defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023” and sought their removal or withholding. The second notice was submitted on November 2 at 8.51 am and listed 40 URLs. These included 37 individual posts and the entire X accounts of IFF, SFLC and GeoBlockedIndia. The provisions cited in the Delhi Police notices relate to criminal defamation and the removal of unlawful online content. The stated reason in the second notice read: “The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours.” Section 356 of the BNS deals with criminal defamation and prescribes punishment for statements made with the intention of harming a person’s reputation. Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules lays down the procedure for intermediaries, including social media platforms, to remove or disable access to unlawful content following legally recognised government or court directions.
